etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English crue, from Old French creue (“an increase, recruit, military reinforcement”), the feminine past participle of creistre (“grow”), from Latin crescere (“to arise, grow”).

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Any company of people; an assemblage; a throng.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book I, Canto IV”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 7:
quote.text: There a noble crew / Of Lordes and Ladies stood on every side.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book IV”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Faithful to whom? to thy rebellious crew?

definitions.definition: A group of people (often staff) manning and operating a large facility or piece of equipment such as a factory, ship, boat, airplane, or spacecraft.

quote.citation: 1905, H. G. Wells, The Empire of the Ants:
quote.text: He saw now clearly that the sole crew of the vessel was these two dead men, and though he could not see their faces, he saw by their outstretched hands, which were all of ragged flesh, that they had been subjected to some strange exceptional process of decay.

quote.citation: 2023 November 29, Paul Clifton, “West is best in the Highlands”, in RAIL, number 997, pages 37-38:
quote.text: There's a change of driver halfway at Crianlarich. Glasgow crews bring the 35-year-old Class 156 north, then wait to take over the next train back south. Crews from Mallaig, Oban and Fort William take their trains from the coast to Crianlarich and swap over. There's a tiny rest room on the platform, with a microwave and a sink, while they wait. Some drivers are signed all the way to the city. Most are not.

definitions.definition: A group of people working together on a task.
(art) The group of workers on a dramatic production who are not part of the cast.
(informal, often derogatory) A close group of friends.
(often derogatory) A set of individuals lumped together by the speaker.

quote.citation: 1861 William Weston Patton, (version of) John Brown's Body
quote.text:
He captured Harper’s Ferry, with his nineteen men so few,
And frightened "Old Virginny" till she trembled thru and thru;
They hung him for a traitor, they themselves the traitor crew,
But his soul is marching on.

quote.citation: 1950, Bernard Nicholas Schilling, Conservative England and the Case Against Voltaire‎[1], page 266:
quote.text: Malignant principles bear fruit in kind and the Revolution did no more than practice what men had been taught by the abandoned crew of philosophers.

definitions.definition: (scouting) A group of Rovers.
(slang, hip-hop) A hip-hop or b-boying group.

quote.text: And Jay cuts the records every day of the week / And we are the crew that can never be meek

quote.citation: 1988 February 7, Carly Darling, “L.A.—The Second Deffest City of Hip-Hop”, in Los Angeles Times‎[2]:
quote.text: The most popular and critically acclaimed rap and deejay “crews”—Run-D.M.C., Whodini, L.L. Cool J, the Beastie Boys, the Fat Boys, Public Enemy, Full Force, Salt & Pepa, Afrika Bambaataa, Kurtis Blow, Mantronix, U.T.F.O., et al.—were spawned on that city's streets.

quote.citation: 2003, Jennifer Guglielmo, Salvatore Salerno, Are Italians White?‎[3], →ISBN, page 150:
quote.text: We decided we needed another rapper in the crew and spent months looking.

quote.citation: 2016, Sophy Smith, Hip-Hop Turntablism, Creativity and Collaboration, Routledge, →ISBN, page 10:
quote.text: In b-boying culture, a group of b-boys or b-girls who dance and battle together are referred to as a crew.

quote.citation: 2021, Jehnie I. Burns, Mixtape Nostalgia: Culture, Memory, and Representation, page 138:
quote.text: […]  mutating into all-star line-ups of emcees spitting hot bars over familiar beats, then to a single crew spitting bars over familiar beats, then eventually to a single crew (or artist) spitting bars over unfamiliar beats.

definitions.definition: (rowing) A rowing team manning a single shell.

quote.text: If a crew feather much under water, it is a good plan to seat them in a row on a bench, and give each man a stick to handle as an oar.

definitions.definition: A group of people together
(plural: crew) A member of the crew of a vessel or plant.
(art, plural: crew) A worker on a dramatic production who is not part of the cast.
(nautical, plural: crew) A member of a ship's company who is not an officer.
A person in a crew
(sports, rowing, US, uncountable) The sport of competitive rowing.

quote.text: The University of Virginia belongs to the Atlantic Coast Conference and competes interscholastically in basketball, baseball, crew, cross country, fencing, football, golf, indoor track, lacrosse, polo, soccer, swimming, tennis, track, and wrestling.

quote.citation: 1989, Benjamin Spock, Mary Morgan, Spock on Spock‎[5], →ISBN, page 71:
quote.text: Two Andover classmates, Al Wilson and Al Lindley, both went out for crew in our freshman year at Yale.

definitions.definition: (transitive and intransitive) To be a member of a vessel's crew
To be a member of a work or production crew
To supply workers or sailors for a crew

quote.text: The seafood companies crewed huge trawlers with new fishermen, many of whom were fish-plant workers, since much of the work on board a modern trawler is fish processing.

quote.citation: 2003, Kirk C. Jenkins, The Battle Rages Higher‎[6], →ISBN, page 42:
quote.text: Steele crewed the boat with men from his own regiment and volunteers from John Wood's detachment.

definitions.definition: (nautical) To do the proper work of a sailor
(nautical) To take on, recruit (new) crew

quote.text: The two ships will be crewing in the latter half of September.

definitions.definition: (British, archaic) simple past of crow (“make the characteristic sound of a rooster”).

quote.citation: 1859, Edward Fitzgerald, The Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám: The Astronomer-Poet of Persia, page 1:
quote.text: And, as the Cock crew, those who stood beforeThe Tavern shouted — "Open then the Door!You know how little while we have to stay,And, once departed, may return no more."

quote.citation: 2004, Gillian Cross, On the Edge‎[8], →ISBN, page 7:
quote.text: Between the shippon and the pig-crew, with the wind blowing over from the vegetable ground.
